newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico finances impress but leaks steal thunder.
newsitem.headline: Mexico finances impress but leaks steal thunder.

text.p: Economists, dissecting a raft of data on Mexico's second quarter public sector finances, said the headline numbers were impressive although earlier leaks stole much of their thunder.
In particular analysts said they were cheered by the improved picture they painted of rising tax receipts and falling debt levels.

"Most eye-catching is the total net public debt -- 27.3 percent is a pretty good number," said Denis Parisien, Latin America economist at Bankers Trust, adding that the figure had plunged from about 44 percent over the past two years.
"To be below the 30 percent barrier is a pretty impressive feat and highlights how well they have operated on the debt profile," he added.
Javier Murcio, director of emerging markets for Latin America at CSFB, agreed, saying that the debt figure showed a clear improvement in the government's financial position.

Improving the nation's debt profile was one of the main planks of the March 1995 stabilisation program designed to haul Mexico back from recession after a shock peso devaluation plunged it into crisis in December 1994.
But tax receipt levels, though robust, were almost a let-down after a number of figures that emerged in the preceding weeks.
"The headline numbers were an anticlimax because so much was leaked beforehand," Parisien said. "We heard that tax receipts were up 15 or 18 percent, but they came out at 11.1 percent."
But in real terms that level was not a disappointment.
"Eleven point one percent is a good number," he said, adding tax receipts were growing at an even stronger rate than the economy as a whole.
Second quarter growth in gross domestic product will be announced on Tuesday and analysts, revising forecasts upwards upwards, are widely expecting a level of at least 5.9 percent.
Economists were also pleased to see the overall surplus showing an increase from the year's first quarter.
"The surplus was 18.371 billion pesos, compared with the first quarter which was 6.354 billion. They did increase their overall surplus in the second quarter," one economist said.
The second quarter number is widely expected to be the last that registers a surplus, before the country moves into quarterly deficits with increased spending in the second half.
However analysts say Mexico should still be able to fulfil official forecasts for a slight surplus of 0.5 percent of GDP by year-end.
The finance ministry explained the increased surplus by noting rising tax revenues and lower costs involved in servicing the government debt.
"That has outstripped the increase in primary spending," Parisien said.
